Appropriate action could include deleting the term from the specification of goods or replacing it with a more acceptable term. One such example would be replacing champagne, where it is being used to describe the style of wine, with sparkling wine."}],"answer":"I cannot determine whether “champagne” can remain in your particular application's goods list.

The general Manual practice—not legislation—is that protected terms appearing in the goods specification will not usually result in a ground for rejection, but specifications containing them should be carefully considered. [TMM/Part32B/3#1]

If a term is clearly inconsistent with the application, the examiner should raise it with the applicant. Appropriate action may include deletion or replacement. The Manual expressly gives replacing “champagne”, when used to describe the style of wine, with “sparkling wine” as an example. Describing style is therefore not, by itself, an assurance that the term may be retained. [TMM/Part32B/3#1]

The supplied legislation does not directly answer whether such a term may remain in the goods list; this guidance rests on the Manual passage."}
